title: Schools built using private money cost executive an extra £1bn
summary: The schools in Belfast, Co Down, Co Antrim and Co Londonderry were all built in the early 2000s using the Private Finance Initiative model.
full_text:
The Northern Ireland Executive will pay over £1bn more for 19 schools than they actually cost to build.

The schools in Belfast, County Down, County Antrim, County Tyrone and County Londonderry were all built in the early 2000s using the Private Finance Initiative (PFI) model.

That meant the executive did not pay for the new buildings but contracted firms to build and maintain them.

The Education Minister Paul Givan told BBC News NI that his department was still paying millions of pounds for the contracts. He also said that he believed the PFI scheme was "flawed."

The PFI model was used to build hospitals, schools, roads and prisons across the UK, but has faced criticism over huge repayment costs to taxpayers.

It can leave governments and public bodies paying billions in long-term charges over 25-30 years, well above the original value of the buildings.

The deals for the 19 school buildings were entered into by the Northern Ireland Executive and not by the schools themselves.

In an answer to an assembly question from the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) assembly member Michelle McIlveen, the Education Minister Paul Givan detailed the schools built using PFI contracts and the costs associated with them.

The original value of the 19 schools in Belfast, Bangor, Derry, Downpatrick, Carryduff, Comber, Portglenone, Strabane and Dundonald was £366m when they were built.

But, according to Department of Education (DE) figures, it is estimated that the executive will pay over £1.5bn by the time the contracts end in the 2030s.

In 2025/26 alone Stormont paid almost £60m towards the 19 schools.

In a report into PFI in 2014, the Northern Ireland Audit Office (NIAO) said that while the scheme had "helped deliver improvements to public services and infrastructure", it would have a significant impact on Stormont's budget until the 2030s.

The education minister said that given the constraints on the education budget, he had considered whether PFI was a "more effective way" to build more schools.

"All of the assessment has come back to say 'no it isn't'," he said.

"You end up paying far more over the lifetime of that school build.

"We have a legacy now of schools that were built under PFI arrangements and they are hugely costly to the taxpayer."

Givan said the PFI policy was wider than Northern Ireland and had been heavily used by the Labour government in the UK in the early 2000s, "and it spilled over into Northern Ireland as well".

"It isn't something I would do," he said.

"But we are living with the consequences of significant expenditure for what was a Public Finance Initiative scheme that I believe was flawed at the time.

"There are ongoing contracts to provide maintenance to those schools that were built under PFI so it wasn't just the initial start-up one-off capital cost.

"There was a contract entered into for a significant period of time to provide the ongoing maintenance and that is hugely costly and having an impact on our budget."

Stormont ministers are yet to agree a budget for 2026/27 but there have been a range of cuts and savings measures in education including a rise in school meal prices and the axing of some school services.

title: Pupils served life lessons from pickleball-playing pensioners
summary: Pickleball and pensioners are helping A-Level students in Belfast learn beyond their school classroom.
full_text:
Career advice and life lessons over a game of pickleball?

That's what students are being served up every week at a club for pensioners. And the elders, who can certainly keep up with them on the competitive front, get to hear about their lives.

The pupils are studying for their A-levels at Breda Academy - which is near the large Belvoir estate on the outskirts of south Belfast - and every Friday, a group of them head to the estate's pensioners club.

Anna, 18, told BBC News NI that making lunch and playing games with the pensioners was something she looked forward to.

"A lot of them speak to me about job experiences they had and give me advice on university and going into careers," she said.

"They're really lovely people and are always giving you advice about life."

Linda Woods, who is a keen pickleball player, said the club was a bridge between the generations.

"It' good to get to know the young and what they're at and what they're doing and it's great that they come," she said.

"Older people have experience of things and it's really good for older people to know what younger people are going through."

Deborah, 17, said: "It's good to help, help clean, help cook, just make sure the pensioners are having a fun time.

"Some of them are really competitive in pickleball!"

She is also helping decorate the hall for Christmas, with the pupils often lending a hand beyond Fridays.

Alison Breadon is the family support worker in Belvoir Community Association and she said the teenagers would often volunteer to help out at events.

"We do a bingo social on a Friday for the pensioners so the children come down, they help us prepare the meals, usually a chicken dinner, soup or stew," she said.

"There's also a wee over-60s club on a Friday here and the children get heavily involved with the pensioners.

"They play pickleball, they play table tennis and they can go in and out of the gym as well."

title: Climate summits need radical reform – here’s how to transform global negotiations
summary: The collapse of Cop31 may become a historical opportunity for global climate governance to tackle its structural problems.
full_text:
The recent failure of the UN climate summit, Cop31, went beyond already gloomy expectations. Yet this political and diplomatic catastrophe may become a historical opportunity for global climate governance to tackle its structural problems.

It is a miracle that Cop climate summits have survived and grown for 31 years, with all decisions needing unanimous consensus from all 195 nations or parties. Cops have produced some positive results such as the 2015 Paris climate agreement to cut greenhouse gases. But now it’s time for radical reform. A reform that must not only abolish unanimity, but also make the Cop capable of engaging a strong enough coalition of interests to advance the climate change agenda.

Where could that start? What kind of alliance does such a reform need? A recent conference on the global governance of climate change provides some answers.

Ending unanimity

Cop has probably been killed by a contradiction. The first Cop in 1995 – chaired by Angela Merkel, then Germany’s young environment minister – was regulated by a UN law. This was the Framework Convention on Climate Change, which envisaged that decisions had to be taken by consensus or, if that wasn’t possible, by two-thirds of the parties (each state of the world is a “party”). This law, known as draft rule 42, was never accepted or rejected, leaving Cop trapped in the unanimity trap.

In 2010, this was enough for Bolivia alone to object to risk derailing the entire negotiation. It is a trap because countries have naturally different interests. Most developing countries are highly exposed to climate change and do not contribute much to the problem; some others not only benefit from oil production but also from global warming itself (notably Russia, as Arctic trade routes open up due to ice melting).

Most other traditional UN institutions do not operate under such strict consensus: the General Assembly (the main policymaking body of the UN), Unesco (the UN’s Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation) and the World Health Organization all vote with a qualified two-thirds majority on important matters.

So unanimity must be abolished. But that is not enough. Cop also manages to be both inefficient and not inclusive enough of the actors that matter a lot in achieving the goals of a climate change agenda. The parties include the tiny country of San Marino yet there’s no representation from megacities like Mumbai or Seattle – cities which may be exposed to climate disaster and host some of the solutions.

A new annual conference called Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels was a significant attempt to move beyond the Cop gridlock. In 2026, 57 countries joined the first meeting in Santa Marta, Colombia after realising at Cop30 last year in Brazil, that, by “consensus”, Cop cannot even agree on the need for a roadmap to end dependence on fossil fuels. And yet even shrinking the number of parties to a quarter of Cop’s total was not enough to get beyond the acknowledgement of such a necessity: the final document did not indicate any timeline nor commit countries to specific targets.

It is too early to say that the Santa Marta process won’t work. But I would argue that it was a mistake not to invite certain nations, namely India and China and the US (although representatives from California did attend).

It was also risky to start the conference with a declaration (issued by Colombia’s then president, Gustavo Petro about the inadequacy of capitalism to stop climate change. Capitalism may be a form of governing economy as primitive as fossil fuels, but to start from such a principle unnecessarily alienates leaders of other countries and business.

Coalition of the willing

Another way to bring together countries and political sides that may have different visions of the world yet share common energy interests is to invite all countries that may respond positively to two simple questions: “Are you interested in developing within two years and sharing your plan to reduce in your country (or city or region) the percentage of energy consumption coming from fossil fuels? If so, are you willing to support each other in building the necessary supply chains and financial facilities to improve that target?”

This may inspire politically diverse local and national governments and business leaders to gradually join what would become a concrete problem-solving exercise. Common ground could hopefully be found in their shared interest to reduce energy dependency and mitigate climate risks.

Read more: What does climate adaptation actually mean? An expert explains

Once most of the net importers of fossil fuels are aligned, the net exporters (including some members of Opec, the oil producers’ cartel) may also commit. This is the sort of coalition of the willing that we need: an alliance capable of increasing its scope and delivering results.

As director of the thinktank Vision, I recently convened the fifth conference on global governance of climate change, held in Venice, Italy, in October 2026, titled Beyond Cop. Over three days, international delegates produced a strong proposal on how to reform Cop. The proposal was authored by professors and students including Kalypso Nikolaidis, chair in global affairs, and Helena Marchall, a masters student, both at the School of Transnational Governance of the European University Institute.

The conference proposes looking beyond ideologies, pre-defined agendas, cognitive biases and siloed thinking that make it difficult for politicians, business and academics to solve complex questions. One suggested change is to make Venice a permanent hub for a new global governance of climate adaptation (the practical steps to prepare for the consequences of a changing climate). This would help drive action and avoid the risk of focusing primarily on mitigation (cutting greenhouse gas emissions to achieve net zero).

We need courage, vision and pragmatism. These are the ingredients to respond to existential threats.

title: 'Fake PhD' controversy stokes student unease in Galway University
summary: Graduates of the University of Galway's journalism and Global Media programmes fear a 'fake PhD' controversy could damage the reputation of their degrees.
full_text:
Kansas native Corey Jackson spent over €20,000 for one year's tuition fees at the University of Galway.

"I wish I had some of it back," he says ruefully. "As far as the quality of education goes, it could have been better."

Mr Jackson, 41, worked in corporate communications in the United States for 15 years before beginning a one-year Master of Arts degree in Global Media in 2025. He graduated on Tuesday.

Recent Prime Time revelations that Tom Felle, a high-profile University of Galway academic and disinformation expert who developed the university's Global Media undergraduate and postgraduate programmes, had falsely claimed to have a PhD, have only added to Mr Jackson’s disenchantment.

Mr Felle’s claim that he had a doctorate in journalism from London's City University (now City St George's) "blows my mind," Mr Jackson says.

Other graduates told Prime Time they are worried that, because of Mr Felle's central role as head of the Department of Journalism and Media until last year, his actions will have tainted their degree.

"Does it make our degree less valuable? I think it does. Are [employers] going to think that we got our degree from a fake doctor?" a recent graduate in journalism said.

Read more: Galway university 'fake news' expert claims fake doctorate

Documents seen by Prime Time show that student disgruntlement at the University of Galway's Journalism and Global Media programmes predate the current controversy.

Prime Time has seen copies of six group complaints by students of journalism and global media sent to college management in the period 2023-2026.

It's understood that a seventh is being prepared in the wake of the Tom Felle controversy.

Those complaints refer to "systemic" and "longstanding" issues, including poor organisation and limited opportunities for practical learning.

While complainants often stress the expertise and dedication of many lecturers, a common complaint from Global Media students is about access to facilities, work placements and student exchange programmes, as well as disruption caused by "sudden, unexplained staff departures."

Mr Jackson feels he was misled by the university’s prospectus. One of the reasons he chose Galway for his MA was that he was "hoping for a shepherded introduction to the Irish jobs market."

In its literature marketing the course, University of Galway states that "Placements are arranged with a wide range of partners, including NGOs, international organisations, policy institutes, communications agencies, cultural organisations, and media outlets."

In reality, Mr Jackson says simply that there were "no internships available" for him.

Brittany Brooker, another Global Media MA student from the US, who has worked in public relations for almost a decade, said that instead of placements being arranged, "Everyone was on their own..."

The 31-year-old Virginia native said that, originally, the MA students were told that companies "come to" the university and ask for graduates.

"Then the conversation shifted from 'everyone comes to us’ to ‘you should try to reach out to NGOs or communications departments.’ "

Ms Brooker who, like Mr Jackson, graduated on Tuesday, also said that access to production facilities like broadcast studios to "improve our skills" was lacking.

Tuition fees for the one-year Master’s degree in Global Media and Communication are not cheap, currently €21,300 for non-EU students like Ms Brooker and Mr Jackson and €11,000 for EU students.

Of the six group student complaints seen by Prime Time, one was from fourth-year Global Media students in November 2024.

It stated: "Over the last three years, and specifically in the last couple of months, we have clearly articulated the multitude of worries we hold about our education at the University of Galway to those we thought would listen. However, it appears that our voices have not been heard, our problems dismissed and accountability has yet to be taken."

The five-page letter named six lecturers as "amazing" but listed an array of structural grievances – "...the course curriculum lacks depth and rigour, and it is structured around modules that do not go hand in hand, creating a completely disjointed learning experience for students."

The letter stated that there was insufficient practical learning and that "the organisation of our Erasmus and work placement was a disgrace."

The complaint letter was signed by over 30 students, representing the overwhelming majority of students taking Global Media as a core subject.

One student who signed that letter told Prime Time: "I felt misled. People felt underqualified on graduating, we didn’t feel prepared."

Another complaint - by second year students of Global Media in May 2024 - alleged that "the absence of a structured curriculum and clear learning outcomes leaves students feeling uncertain about their academic journey and ill-prepared for future endeavours."

It also referred to "unfulfilled promises" of "guest lectures, practical workshops and additional resources."

That letter was signed by 48 students, representing around half of the class.

Of the other group complaints seen by Prime Time, two were sent by a class rep on behalf of students, and two complaints were sent anonymously as a class cohort, one by the MA in Journalism students in December 2023 and the other by MA Global Media students this year.

The latter complaint, composed by Ms Brooker and fellow students, was emailed to senior figures in the university in September and a follow-up was sent last month. It was signed off as "The Graduating MA Global Media & Communication Cohort," and sent from an anonymous email address.

It was emailed anonymously, because, the letter said, "many of us genuinely fear professional or academic repercussions for speaking openly."

The letter went on to say: "We do not intend to criticise individuals, but to highlight systemic issues that we believe are affecting students, the programme's reputation, and ultimately the university's ability to attract and retain future international students."

The complaint said that: "The handbook describes employability as a core component of the programme, highlighting internships, employability training, CV preparation, interview preparation and collaboration with the Careers Development Centre."

It added that: "Many students' experiences did not reflect these commitments. The majority of our cohort received little meaningful support with: securing internships; identifying communications-specific employment opportunities; introductions to employers; networking events designed for communications professionals; graduate job applications within Ireland."

It adds: "The single organised field experience was primarily journalism-focused rather than relevant to the communications careers many students intended to pursue."

Prime Time spoke to veteran academics lecturing at three other Irish universities who said that they had never witnessed this type of student group complaint about course quality at their own universities.

We told the University of Galway that we were aware of at least five group complaints [after our query, that figure rose to six] by students of Journalism and Global Media and asked it to comment.

In its response, the university said that: "The reference to ‘five group complaints’ is completely inaccurate."

"A complaint made in the 2023/24 academic year was given thorough consideration through formal processes and it was not upheld." It also noted that: "Tom Felle was not head of discipline in 2023/24." Mr Felle was in the United States at the time on a Fulbright scholarship.

"No other complaints were made in 2023/24. No further complaints have been made since then."

However, not only were there other complaints, formally submitted, but the university’s Discipline of Journalism and Media formally replied in detail to most of them.

Prime Time has seen responses in relation to four of the six group student complaints which emanated from postgraduate and undergraduate students of journalism and global media since 2023.

All four were responded to by staff at the Department of Journalism, including the MA Journalism complaint in 2023 that was sent anonymously. One of the four complaints was also subsequently dealt with by the university's Student Complaint's Board.

The board’s decision in that case did not find in favour of the students "in relation to concerns regarding academic malpractice, mismanagement of student fees and neglect of student welfare," but it acknowledged that "general staffing absences caused by various periods of leave... did have a negative impact on students."

It appears the university only records a complaint as a complaint if it is referred to the Students Complaints Board, which is the third stage of the University's Student Complaints Process.

In circumstances where a formal letter from a group of students or a student representative is submitted containing concerns or grievances, it appears that, unless the complaint is subsequently referred to the Student Complaint's Board, it is not recorded as a complaint even in circumstances when it is formally responded to by the department.

The University also said in its response that: "If an issue is raised by any student in relation to teaching and learning it is treated with utmost importance and the student is advised of the option to make a formal complaint. If a formal complaint is submitted, the Dean of Students will carry out a preliminary assessment, which can include evidence gathering. If the complaint is deemed appropriate for resolution, the Dean of Students will refer the complaint to a dedicated central board for investigation and adjudication."

In some of the six formal group complaints since 2023, students have suggested or requested that they be financially compensated.

Although these recent requests were denied, back in 2018, the university, then known as NUI Galway, did refund fees to third- and fourth-year journalism students after complaints.

Tom Felle was hired to clean up the reputation of the poorly performing Journalism Department in 2018, four years before he claimed he was awarded a PhD from City University in London.

Some students told Prime Time that, aside from grievances over the quality of education provided, they are also angry because the university has not publicly addressed the Tom Felle ‘fake PhD’ controversy.

title: Amid rising costs, Keralam’s aided primary school headteachers seek higher fund allocation for noon meal scheme
summary: Prices of eggs, milk, groceries, vegetables, and LPG cylinder refills have gone up considerably in recent times
full_text:
Headteachers of aided primary schools in Keralam are concerned that the noon meal scheme is becoming a financial burden on them amid rising prices of essential commodities, particularly eggs and milk.

N.C. Abdullakutty, State president, and M.I. Ajikumar, general secretary, Kerala Private Primary Headmasters’ Association, say the government allocates ₹6.78 per student in the lower primary (LP) sections (Classes 1 to 4) and ₹10.17 per student in the upper primary (UP) sections (Classes 5 to 8). Additionally, as per a supplementary nutrition programme, the schools are required to distribute one egg a day, and 150 ml of milk on two other days, every week.

The sanctioned rates are ₹6 per egg and ₹52 per litre of milk. In the open market, however, the price ranges from ₹8 to ₹10 per egg, while milk costs between ₹65 and ₹70 a litre if it is procured from milk cooperative societies, and ₹60 a litre through Milma. Though the price of eggs has come down a bit in recent days, this situation may not continue for long, the teachers say.

Mr. Abdullakutty points out that if the price of Milma milk is raised by ₹10 a litre, the noon meal scheme would have to be implemented while incurring a loss of ₹18 to ₹25 a litre.

High gas prices

The headteachers also claim that the price rise of other commodities such as vegetables and groceries and the frequent hikes in LPG cylinder refills are also burning a hole in their pockets. The price of non-domestic cooking gas has doubled compared with last year. A 19-kg non-domestic LPG cylinder now costs around ₹2,870, which can last up to two weeks.

For LP schools with fewer than 100 students, the allocated funds are insufficient to cover even the cost of the monthly gas cylinder refill, let alone vegetables and groceries, they say. Most often, the headteachers are forced to carry on the financial burden on their own. Some of them are now depending on sponsorships and financial help from the PTA.

“The above-mentioned rates were fixed around five-six years ago. We are demanding that the government increase the funds for the noon meal scheme. The allowance for eggs should be adjusted to reflect the current market rates and the allocation for milk be raised to ₹60 a litre. Also, the availability of LPG cylinders should be guaranteed,” Mr. Abdullakutty says.

The association has also urged the government to implement a community kitchen system, similar to those in some neighbouring States, and to relieve headteachers of the responsibilities associated with the scheme.

title: China looks to deepen international university partnerships
summary:
China is seeking to strengthen international education partnerships, with Thailand taking centre stage as the country of honour for the first time at this year's CACIE conference.

The post China looks to deepen international university partnerships appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
Connecting Chinese universities with overseas partners was a key focus of the 27th China Annual Conference & Expo for International Education (CACIE), held in Beijing.

Organised by the China Education Association for International Exchange (CEAIE), the event brought together more than 6,000 delegates representing over 2,000 educational institutions from more than 70 countries and regions.

CEAIE said in a statement that by “breaking down barriers through openness and pooling strength through cooperation, this year’s conference provided end-to-end support for two-way engagement—helping Chinese institutions expand their partnerships overseas while connecting international partners with opportunities in China—injecting fresh momentum into the shared development of global education”.

Nearly 160 international institutions participated in matchmaking sessions designed to facilitate new partnerships with Chinese universities, including dedicated sessions with institutions from the UK, US, Thailand and Russia.

Meanwhile, the conference saw the launch of the inaugural Report on the Development of International Cooperation and Exchange in China’s Higher Education.

The report examines trends in China’s international higher education partnerships and models of international education, putting forward proposals for more sustainable and mutually beneficial collaboration.

Set to be published annually, it aims to inform government decision-making and support Chinese and overseas universities in developing international partnerships.

This year’s conference provided end-to-end support for two-way engagement—helping Chinese institutions expand their partnerships overseas while connecting international partners with opportunities in China—injecting fresh momentum into the shared development of global education

China Education Association for International Exchange (CEAIE)

Thailand served as the conference’s country of honour for the first time, a role acknowledged in a July joint statement by the Chinese and Thai governments

A delegation of 16 Thai universities showcased opportunities for study, research and institutional collaboration, reflecting efforts to deepen educational ties between the two countries.

Discussions throughout the conference also explored emerging areas of international education, including digital education, internationalisation at home and microcredentials.

The accompanying China Education Expo drew more than 420 institutions and organisations from 35 countries and regions. The five-city tour began in Beijing before continuing to Wuhan, Chengdu, Guangzhou and Shanghai.

title: After a decade of growth, what’s next for Hungary as a study destination?
summary:
Hungary's universities have spent more than a decade building the country up as a study destination. Now the sector says the next challenge is keeping international talent once students graduate.

The post After a decade of growth, what’s next for Hungary as a study destination? appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
Following the recent Western Balkans Forum, hosted by the University of Pécs for the first time, The PIE News caught up with stakeholders to discuss how Hungary’s international education sector is evolving, and the challenges ahead.

The government-funded Stipendium Hungaricum scholarship launched in 2013 and is backed by about 100 bilateral agreements with other governments. Sector leaders say it has put Hungary on the map for students around the world.

“It became probably one of the most comprehensive government-financed scholarship programs in the world over the past 10-plus years,” said István Tarrósy, director of the International Center and professor of political science at the University of Pécs. “That really boosted in the mindset of a lot of young people across the globe to come to Hungary as a non-traditional destination.”

Interest appears to be rising further. According to Studyportals data, Hungary’s share of student interest in on-campus bachelor’s and master’s degrees has risen 24% since the beginning of April. Nigeria, Pakistan and Kenya have seen the sharpest rises in interest in Hungary over that period.

“At least based on the data that we have, especially for Hungary, the interest is growing,” said Rob van Schaijk, business unit manager for UKI & EMEA at Studyportals. He said this is in line with a wider shift: “Some of the interest in the traditional top four is declining, and [students] do look at other options in Europe and Asia… that includes the Western Balkans and Hungary as well.”

Some of the interest in the traditional top four is declining, and [students] do look at other options in Europe and Asia… that includes the Western Balkans and Hungary as well

Rob van Schaijk, Studyportals

At Pécs, international enrolment has grown from about 2,400 students in 2015 to more than 6,000 from 150 countries. Some of that growth was driven by a national Modern Cities program, which the university negotiated to focus on internationalisation.

But Tarrósy said the focus is now shifting. “Not only the number now matters for us in 2026, but how we can sustain this, and how we can focus more on the quality students,” he said.

He said diversity is a priority, partly to avoid relying too heavily on any one market. “It’s more important for us to have a rewarding, encouraging, supportive intercultural learning environment.”

Asked why students choose Hungary, Tarrósy pointed to competitive fees, quality teaching, safety and good graduate outcomes. “Most of them go back home… my South African students right away got a job,” he said. “We have in the immediate neighbourhood the ongoing Russia-Ukraine war, but we have been one of the most secure places.”

He said practical barriers remain, including regional air links. New regular flights between Munich and Pécs “will help a lot”, he said. Germany sends Pécs its largest group of students because of the university’s German-taught medicine degree.

Van Schaijk said Hungary’s value could become a stronger selling point as the cost of living rises. “In times where life is getting more expensive in many parts of the world… the price sensitivity is increasing,” he said. Fees in Hungary and the Western Balkans are “generally a little bit lower” while “quality of education can be very high”.

The challenge, he said, is “to turn that perception… that low tuition fee does not mean low quality, and really turn that into value”.

Brand awareness is the bigger hurdle. “When international students start thinking about studying in Europe, Hungary or the Western Balkans in general is not [a destination] that comes to mind at the start,” he said. He sees a regional role for his university and country: “What Pécs aims to do, or what it can do, is really bridge the Western Balkans to the rest of Europe.”

Hungary also faces a demographic squeeze. Its fertility rate is low, its population is ageing, and Tarrósy said “hundreds of thousands” of people, many of them young graduates, left during “the previous 16 years” for the UK, Germany and Austria.

“From a very objective labour market perspective, we would need our own graduates – and why not our own graduates, even from Nigeria or from Pakistan or from wherever?” he said. “We were training them, we know them, so they know us.”

But he warned that “the immigration regime is still challenging”. He said the political climate of recent years had not created “a conducive environment” for keeping international students after graduation.

He said it is too soon to tell whether the new government, which has been in office for about six months, has changed things for international students.

Van Schaijk agreed that keeping graduates is not yet high enough on the agenda. Asked whether ministers and universities are thinking about it, he said: “Probably not enough yet.” He said the answer starts with the curriculum. Universities building English-taught programs should “involve local industries”, which “ultimately makes it easier for people to potentially stay”.

He is more hopeful than Tarrósy about the new government. “There’s also some political optimism in getting a new government in Hungary, which hopefully is more open to international students,” he said. “There’s been a wave of right-wing populism in Europe, which is not always great for international students.”

Tarrósy has three priorities for policymakers. First, Hungary must stay competitive on fees, quality and learning environment.

Second, it needs smarter immigration rules. “I wouldn’t say more flexible rules, but certainly more adaptive rules of immigration, so that we can foster our graduates to stay if they want, and if we would like them to stay,” he said.

Third, he wants stronger government support for universities in European University Alliances, so they can win more Horizon, and other, research funding. Pécs is a founding member of the European Digital UniverCity (EDUC) alliance since 2019.

“In Hungary we should pay more attention to such European frameworks,” he said.

title: MFHEA: Connecting English language learning with higher education in Malta
summary:
MFHEA CEO discusses Malta's growing international education sector, quality assurance and the potential to strengthen pathways from English language learning into further and higher education.

The post MFHEA: Connecting English language learning with higher education in Malta appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
1. You hold a significant role at the Malta Further and Higher Education Authority. For our international education audience, could you begin by telling us a little about yourself and your background, and then briefly explain what MFHEA is responsible for and where it sits within Malta’s wider education landscape?

My career has been centred on education, with experience in institutional leadership, vocational education, accreditation and quality assurance. Before becoming CEO of MFHEA, I held leadership positions at MCAST, the Institute of Tourism Studies and the Archbishop’s Seminary, and served as CEO of the Federation of English Language teaching organisations Malta (FELTOM).

These experiences have helped me understand the sector from different perspectives, including those of institutions, students and the regulator.

MFHEA is Malta’s national authority responsible for regulating further and higher education. Our work includes licensing providers, accrediting programmes against the Malta Qualifications Framework, overseeing quality assurance and supporting the recognition of qualifications.

Our responsibility is to protect students’ interests and confidence in Malta’s education provision, while supporting the sector’s development. We want Malta to offer opportunities for education that are supported by clear standards and credible qualifications.

2. MFHEA’s mandate covers further and higher education, while the ELT sector is primarily overseen by the ELT Council Malta. How do the two bodies work together on quality assurance, and where exactly does MFHEA’s remit begin when it comes to English language provision?

The ELT Council and MFHEA have complementary responsibilities. The ELT Council oversees English language schools, while MFHEA regulates further and higher education provision.

We are currently in discussions about MFHEA recognising the quality assurance work conducted by the ELT Council as part of the process through which English language schools can obtain an MFHEA licence. The intention is to build on the work already undertaken by the Council and facilitate the licensing process for schools wishing to offer accredited further education programmes.

Programme accreditation would remain the responsibility of MFHEA. The proposed recognition concerns institutional quality assurance; programmes submitted for MFHEA accreditation would still need to undergo our programme accreditation process.

This collaboration can help create clearer connections between the two sectors and support schools wishing to develop their educational offering by offering accredited courses.

3. A core part of MFHEA’s work is accreditation against the Malta Qualifications Framework. Could you explain how that process works for a provider—and what MQF accreditation ultimately means for the students who study there?

For a student, the main question is: “What will I learn, and what qualification will I receive?” Accreditation helps give a clear answer.

Before a programme is accredited by MFHEA, we look at what students are expected to learn, how they will be taught and assessed, and the amount of study involved. External experts review the programme, and the institution may need to make improvements before it is approved. Separately, the institution needs a licence confirming that it meets the requirements to operate.

When a programme is accredited against the Malta Qualifications Framework, or MQF, students can understand its level and the learning it represents. This also helps other institutions and employers understand the qualification.

I would encourage students to check the exact course they are choosing, its title, MQF level, credits and who awards the qualification. Think about where you want it to take you, too. If you plan to continue studying or enter a regulated profession, check those entry requirements before enrolling. That helps you choose a programme that fits your goals.

4. Could you walk us through how MFHEA’s external quality assurance process of licensed institutions works in practice—how often institutions are subject to this process, what the audit examines, and what happens when a provider falls short of the required standards?

Licensed institutions normally undergo an external quality assurance audit on a five-year cycle. The purpose is to check whether their quality assurance arrangements are working in practice and to help them improve the education and support students receive.

Audits are conducted against Malta’s National Quality Assurance Framework, which draws on European references, including the Standards and Guidelines for Quality Assurance in the European Higher Education Area (ESG) for higher education and the European Quality Assurance Reference Framework for Vocational Education and Training (EQAVET) for vocational education and training.

The process includes reviewing institutional evidence and speaking with management, staff and students. It examines teaching and assessment, academic integrity, student support, resources and the accuracy of public information. It also considers how the institution is managed, how it takes responsibility for quality and how it contributes to society.

Where shortcomings are identified, providers may be required to make improvements within specified timeframes and demonstrate that these have been implemented. Serious or persistent non-compliance can lead to regulatory action affecting their licence.

An audit serves both accountability and quality enhancement. It helps institutions identify what works well and where they need to improve, while keeping student protection and educational standards central throughout the process.

5. Beyond accreditation and quality assurance, what support does MFHEA itself offer to providers?

An important part of our role is helping providers understand the requirements they need to meet. Clear guidance and communication support institutions in developing their provision and maintaining effective quality assurance.

We want an open relationship in which institutions can ask questions and raise concerns, while taking responsibility for the quality of their provision. This contributes to a stronger education sector and a better experience for students.

6. One area where this matters today is students who begin in English language schools and later move into further or higher education. From MFHEA’s perspective, how smooth is that pathway today, and what are Malta’s main advantages there?

Many students choose to study English in Malta as a stepping stone towards further or higher education. Developing their English helps them prepare for programmes taught in the language and meet the English language entry requirements of their chosen institution.

One of Malta’s advantages is that students can begin that journey here and explore opportunities to continue their studies in the same country. They have already become familiar with Malta and gained confidence using English in everyday life.

There is an opportunity to strengthen connections between English language schools and further and higher education institutions. This would help students plan their next steps and understand how their language studies can contribute to their wider educational goals.

These figures cover education delivered from Malta, including students studying online from abroad. They therefore reflect both the international character of our institutions and their wider reach.

Our responsibility is to ensure that growth is supported by quality education, clear information and appropriate student support.

8. Finally, if you could share one message with our international education audience reading this interview—what would you want them to know about studying English in Malta today, and about the pathway it can open into further and higher education?

I would encourage students to see Malta as an education hub where learning English can open opportunities for further and higher education.

For many students, an English language course is the beginning of a longer educational journey. It helps them develop the language skills and confidence needed to continue their studies, while becoming familiar with life in Malta.

My advice is to plan that journey carefully. Explore the institutions and programmes available, check their licensing and accreditation, and understand the entry requirements for the next stage.

Malta has an opportunity to connect the strengths of its English language sector with its further and higher education provision. Our role is to support that opportunity through clear standards and reliable information, so that students can make informed choices about their future.

James Perry-Maia is CEO of the Malta Further and Higher Education Authority (MFHEA), bringing extensive experience in educational leadership, accreditation and quality assurance. title: Eiche und Schilf zugleich: Wie New Work zur resilienten Transformation von Hochschulen beitragen kann
summary:
Hochschulen stehen vor der Herausforderung, Stabilität und Wandel zugleich zu ermöglichen. In ihrem Beitrag zeigt Anne Prill, warum digitale Resilienz mehr bedeutet als Krisenfestigkeit und weshalb New Work nicht als Selbstzweck verstanden werden sollte. Statt einzelner Maßnahmen rückt sie die Frage in den Mittelpunkt, wie Beteiligung, Vertrauen und gemeinsame Handlungsfähigkeit entstehen. Ein Plädoyer dafür, Hochschulen zugleich als Eiche und Schilf zu denken.

The post Eiche und Schilf zugleich: Wie New Work zur resilienten Transformation von Hochschulen beitragen kann appeared first on Hochschulforum Digitalisierung.

Was überlebt einen schweren Sturm besser: die mächtige Eiche oder das flexible Schilf? Auf den ersten Blick scheint die Antwort eindeutig: Das Schilf bewegt sich mit dem Wind, gibt nach und richtet sich anschließend wieder auf. Aber die Eiche steht für etwas, das Hochschulen ebenso brauchen: Verlässlichkeit, Verwurzelung und Schutz vor jedem kurzfristigen Trend. Nur Schilf zu sein hieße, sich jedem Wind anzupassen; nur Eiche zu sein birgt das Risiko, unter zu viel Druck zu brechen. Zukunftsfähigkeit entsteht deshalb nicht aus einem Entweder-oder, sondern aus der Verbindung von Stabilität und Beweglichkeit.

Genau diese Spannung beschreibt die aktuelle Lage der Hochschulen. Digitalisierung und Künstliche Intelligenz verändern Aufgaben und Arbeitsweisen, Fachkräfte fehlen, Budgets sind knapp, bürokratische Strukturen begrenzen Handlungsspielräume. Zugleich sollen Hochschulen innovativ, effizient, nachhaltig und partizipativ sein. Westermann und Budde beschreiben diesen Zustand mit Blick auf die digitale Transformation als Modus einer „permanenten Ad-hoc-Krise“: Hochschulen bleiben zwar reaktionsfähig, verbrauchen dabei aber Innovationskapital und verlieren strategische Gestaltungsfähigkeit. Digitale Resilienz darf deshalb nicht als unverrückbares „Bollwerk“ gegen Wandel missverstanden werden. Sie meint vielmehr die Fähigkeit, Veränderung in die institutionelle DNA zu integrieren und auch unter Störungen souverän handlungsfähig zu bleiben (vgl. Westermann & Budde, 2026, S. 2–5). Für mich folgt daraus: Hochschulen werden unter Druck zukunftsfähig, wenn sie Stabilität sichern und zugleich ihre kollektive Veränderungsfähigkeit stärken. New Work kann dafür einen Orientierungsrahmen bieten.

Wer über New Work spricht, landet schnell bei Homeoffice, hybrider Arbeit oder neuen Bürokonzepten. Der Ursprung des Begriffs ist jedoch grundsätzlicher. Für den Sozialphilosophen Frithjof Bergmann (2020) war New Work keine Methode der Organisationsentwicklung und kein Baukasten flexibler Arbeitsmodelle. Im Zentrum stand die Frage, wie Arbeit dem Menschen dienen, Selbstbestimmung ermöglichen und gesellschaftliche Teilhabe fördern kann.

In der heutigen Organisationspraxis ist der Begriff breiter geworden. Das Fraunhofer IAO (vgl. Hofmann, Piele & Piele, 2019) unterscheidet vier zentrale Entwicklungsrichtungen: die zeitliche und räumliche Flexibilisierung von Arbeit, veränderte Führungs- und Machtstrukturen, die stärkere Bedeutung von Sinn und Werteorientierung sowie agile, projektförmige Organisationsweisen jenseits starrer Silos. New Work ist damit deutlich mehr als die Frage, von wo aus gearbeitet wird.

Diese Perspektive ist wichtig, weil einzelne Maßnahmen leicht mit Transformation verwechselt werden. Homeoffice, Coworking, agile Methoden oder neue Beteiligungsformate können sinnvoll sein. Sie entfalten ihre Wirkung aber nicht automatisch. Entscheidend ist, ob sie in eine Organisationsentwicklung eingebettet sind, die zur jeweiligen Hochschule, ihren Aufgaben und ihren Menschen passt (vgl. Prill, 2025; Jongmanns & Lübcke, 2025). New Work ist damit für mich kein Endpunkt, sondern ein möglicher Ausgangspunkt für die größere Frage, wie Hochschulen ihre organisationale Handlungs- und Wandlungsfähigkeit stärken.

Unter Druck suchen Organisationen verständlicherweise nach schnellen Lösungen: neue Tools, neue Prozesse, neue Regeln. In meiner Arbeit mit Hochschulen beobachte ich, dass häufig intensiv darüber diskutiert wird, welche New-Work-Maßnahmen eingeführt werden sollten. Seltener wird gefragt, warum Veränderung überhaupt gelingt oder warum gute Ideen, engagierte Menschen und erfolgreiche Pilotprojekte oft nur punktuell Wirkung entfalten.

Deshalb lohnt sich eine Verschiebung der Perspektive über New Work hinaus. Nicht zuerst: Wie führen wir New Work ein? Sondern: Was braucht es, damit Veränderungen an Hochschulen überhaupt wirksam werden? Diese Frage führt weg vom Maßnahmenkatalog und hin zur besonderen Organisationslogik der Hochschule.

Hochschulen sind keine Unternehmen mit einer durchgängig hierarchischen Steuerung. Sie bestehen aus Fakultäten, Instituten, Fachbereichen, Lehrstühlen und Verwaltungseinheiten mit hoher Eigenständigkeit. In der Organisationsforschung werden sie deshalb als lose gekoppelte Systeme beschrieben (vgl. Weick, 1976). Eine Entscheidung oder Innovation in einem Teil der Hochschule verändert nicht automatisch das gesamte System.

Gerade darin liegt eine produktive Spannung: Dieselbe Autonomie, die lokale Innovation ermöglicht, erschwert ihre hochschulweite Verbreitung. Eine Fakultät kann Neues erproben, während andere Bereiche bewusst an Bewährtem festhalten. Hochschulen sind deshalb zugleich hochinnovativ und hochbeharrlich. Ihre lose Kopplung schützt vor Krisen und ermöglicht Anpassung in einzelnen Teilsystemen. Sie kann aber auch dazu führen, dass vielversprechende Lösungen nicht in die Breite gelangen (vgl. Budde & Prill, 2026). Für die digitale Resilienz kann dieselbe lose Kopplung allerdings zur Achillesferse werden, wenn hochgradig vernetzte Herausforderungen bereichsübergreifende Lösungen erfordern, während Abstimmungswege lang und Zuständigkeiten fragmentiert bleiben (vgl. Westermann & Budde, 2026, S. 5–6).

Wenn Unsicherheit steigt, wächst der Wunsch nach Orientierung. Organisationen reagieren dann häufig mit mehr Kontrolle, zusätzlichen Regeln und engerer Steuerung. Das kann kurzfristig Stabilität schaffen. Es erzeugt jedoch noch keine Veränderungsbereitschaft.

Nachhaltiger Wandel entsteht dort, wo Menschen sich als Teil der Veränderung verstehen: wo sie beteiligt werden, Sinn erkennen, Vertrauen erleben und erfahren, dass sie selbst etwas bewegen können. Hochschulen brauchen selbstverständlich Strategien, Entscheidungen und Führung. Aber in einem lose gekoppelten System lässt sich Transformation nicht einfach verordnen. Meine zugespitzte These lautet deshalb: Mehr Steuerung schafft Stabilität. Beteiligung schafft Veränderungsfähigkeit (vgl. Budde & Prill, 2026).

Hier liegt die Kernaussage dieses Beitrags: New Work wird für Hochschulen dort transformativ, wo die äußere Gestaltung von Arbeit mit der inneren und sozialen Veränderungsfähigkeit verbunden wird. Die Unterscheidung zwischen Outer Work und Inner Work macht diese Verbindung sichtbar. Outer Work bezeichnet die äußere Gestaltung von Arbeit: Strategien, Prozesse, Strukturen, Räume und Werkzeuge. Inner Work richtet den Blick auf die innere und soziale Ebene: Vertrauen, gemeinsame Sinnbildung, Reflexion, psychologische Sicherheit und Verantwortungsübernahme (vgl. Breidenbach & Rollow, 2019). Psychologische Sicherheit ist dabei nicht bloß ein angenehmes Arbeitsklima. Forschung zeigt, dass sie Lernverhalten in Teams unterstützt. Dazu gehört die Offenheit, die nötig ist, um Fehler anzusprechen, Fragen zu stellen und neue Wege zu erproben (vgl. Edmondson, 1999).

Je autonomer die Teilsysteme einer Hochschule sind, desto wichtiger wird Inner Work. Denn kollektive Handlungsfähigkeit entsteht nicht allein dadurch, dass eine Strategie beschlossen wurde. Sie entsteht, wenn Menschen über Fakultäts-, Bereichs- und Statusgrenzen hinweg bereit und in der Lage sind, gemeinsam in eine Richtung zu handeln.

Inner Work ist deshalb an Hochschulen kein „Soft Factor“, sondern Transformationskompetenz. Vertrauen, Sinn und psychologische Sicherheit schaffen die Grundlage dafür, dass aus vielen autonomen Akteur:innen gemeinsames Handeln entstehen kann. Daran lässt sich das Resilienzverständnis von Westermann und Budde (2026) anschließen: Digitale Resilienz wird dort als strategische Metakompetenz beschrieben, die technische, organisationale und individuelle Ebenen miteinander verschränkt. Inner Work deckt diese Ebenen nicht vollständig ab, stärkt aber zentrale individuelle und organisationale Voraussetzungen, um unter Druck handlungsfähig zu bleiben und Wandel aktiv zu gestalten. Unter Druck wird diese Fähigkeit zur strategischen Ressource: Sie ermöglicht Bewegung, ohne die notwendige Stabilität der Organisation aufzugeben.

Drei zentrale Erkenntnisse

Erstens: Resilienz verbindet Stabilität und Anpassungsfähigkeit. Zukunftsfähigkeit zeigt sich weder darin, jede Veränderung sofort zu übernehmen, noch darin, den Status quo möglichst unverändert zu bewahren. Entscheidend ist, tragfähige Strukturen zu schützen und zugleich beweglich genug zu bleiben, um auf neue Herausforderungen zu reagieren und aus ihnen zu lernen.

Zweitens: Transformation lässt sich nicht verordnen. Nachhaltiger Wandel braucht Beteiligung, Kommunikation und gemeinsame Sinnbildung. Strategische Klarheit und Mitgestaltung sind dabei keine Gegensätze, sondern müssen zusammenspielen.

Drittens: Inner Work ist Transformationskompetenz. Vertrauen, Reflexion, Sinn und psychologische Sicherheit sind Voraussetzungen dafür, dass Hochschulangehörige Verantwortung übernehmen und aus lokalen Initiativen kollektive Bewegung entsteht.

Am Ende komme ich zur Ausgangsfrage zurück. Sollten Hochschulen eher Eiche oder Schilf sein? Die Antwort zeichnet sich nun deutlicher ab: Sie müssen beides sein und beide Seiten haben ihre Schattenseiten. Eine Hochschule, die nur Eiche ist, kann Stabilität mit Unbeweglichkeit verwechseln. Eine Hochschule, die nur Schilf ist, droht auf jede neue Technologie oder externe Erwartung reflexartig zu reagieren. Resilienz liegt zwischen diesen Polen: nicht im Bollwerk gegen Veränderung und nicht in permanenter Anpassung, sondern in einer stabilen Wandlungsfähigkeit.

Hochschulen brauchen die Stabilität der Eiche. Forschung und Lehre benötigen Verlässlichkeit. Wissenschaft braucht Freiheit. Institutionen brauchen Identität, Werte und Orientierung. Diese Stabilität schützt vor kurzfristigen Moden und schafft die Basis, auf der Neues überhaupt verantwortungsvoll erprobt werden kann. Gleichzeitig brauchen Hochschulen die Beweglichkeit des Schilfs: die Fähigkeit zu lernen, auf neue Herausforderungen zu reagieren und sich weiterzuentwickeln – ohne dabei jedem Impuls ungeprüft zu folgen.

Transformation bedeutet deshalb nicht, das Alte durch das Neue zu ersetzen. Sie bedeutet, Bedingungen zu schaffen, unter denen Stabilität und Erneuerung über längere Zeit nebeneinander bestehen können – damit Neues wachsen kann, ohne das Bestehende zu entwerten. New Work ist dabei weder Selbstzweck noch Maßnahmenkatalog. Es kann dann einen Beitrag zu resilienter Transformation leisten, wenn es Rahmenbedingungen schafft, in denen Menschen Verantwortung übernehmen, gemeinsam lernen und Wandel gestalten. Hochschulen werden nicht zukunftsfähig, weil sie möglichst viele New-Work-Maßnahmen einführen. Sie werden zukunftsfähig, wenn sie lernen, Wandel gemeinsam zu gestalten.

Anne Prill ist seit 2017 Projektmanagerin für das Hochschulforum Digitalisierung beim CHE Centrum für Hochschulentwicklung. Als Transformationsdesignerin ist sie vor allem für die Themen „Zukunftsorientierte Lernräume“ und „New Work an Hochschulen“ zuständig. Dazu veröffentlicht sie HFD-Arbeitspapiere sowie Artikel und hält Keynotes auf verschiedenen Veranstaltungen. Außerdem initiierte sie das Tandem-Programm „HFDlead“, bei dem sie bundesweit Hochschulleitungen miteinander vernetzt und begleitet. Sie studierte Betriebswirtschaftslehre an der University of Sunderland und Wirtschaft, Europapolitik und Recht an der TH Wildau. Berufsbegleitend absolvierte sie zudem ihren Masterabschluss in Erwachsenenbildung an der TU Kaiserslautern. Seit September 2024 ist sie zertifizierte systemische Transformationsbegleiterin.

Inner Work deckt diese Ebenen nicht vollständig ab, stärkt aber zentrale individuelle und organisationale Voraussetzungen, um unter Druck handlungsfähig zu bleiben und Wandel aktiv zu gestalten. Unter Druck wird diese Fähigkeit zur strategischen Ressource: Sie ermöglicht Bewegung, ohne die notwendige Stabilität der Organisation aufzugeben.

Drei zentrale Erkenntnisse

Erstens: Resilienz verbindet Stabilität und Anpassungsfähigkeit. Zukunftsfähigkeit zeigt sich weder darin, jede Veränderung sofort zu übernehmen, noch darin, den Status quo möglichst unverändert zu bewahren. Entscheidend ist, tragfähige Strukturen zu schützen und zugleich beweglich genug zu bleiben, um auf neue Herausforderungen zu reagieren und aus ihnen zu lernen.

Zweitens: Transformation lässt sich nicht verordnen. Nachhaltiger Wandel braucht Beteiligung, Kommunikation und gemeinsame Sinnbildung. Strategische Klarheit und Mitgestaltung sind dabei keine Gegensätze, sondern müssen zusammenspielen.

Drittens: Inner Work ist Transformationskompetenz. Vertrauen, Reflexion, Sinn und psychologische Sicherheit sind Voraussetzungen dafür, dass Hochschulangehörige Verantwortung übernehmen und aus lokalen Initiativen kollektive Bewegung entsteht.

Am Ende komme ich zur Ausgangsfrage zurück. Sollten Hochschulen eher Eiche oder Schilf sein? Die Antwort zeichnet sich nun deutlicher ab: Sie müssen beides sein und beide Seiten haben ihre Schattenseiten. Eine Hochschule, die nur Eiche ist, kann Stabilität mit Unbeweglichkeit verwechseln. Eine Hochschule, die nur Schilf ist, droht auf jede neue Technologie oder externe Erwartung reflexartig zu reagieren. Resilienz liegt zwischen diesen Polen: nicht im Bollwerk gegen Veränderung und nicht in permanenter Anpassung, sondern in einer stabilen Wandlungsfähigkeit.

Hochschulen brauchen die Stabilität der Eiche. Forschung und Lehre benötigen Verlässlichkeit. Wissenschaft braucht Freiheit. Institutionen brauchen Identität, Werte und Orientierung. Diese Stabilität schützt vor kurzfristigen Moden und schafft die Basis, auf der Neues überhaupt verantwortungsvoll erprobt werden kann. Gleichzeitig brauchen Hochschulen die Beweglichkeit des Schilfs: die Fähigkeit zu lernen, auf neue Herausforderungen zu reagieren und sich weiterzuentwickeln – ohne dabei jedem Impuls ungeprüft zu folgen.

Transformation bedeutet deshalb nicht, das Alte durch das Neue zu ersetzen. Sie bedeutet, Bedingungen zu schaffen, unter denen Stabilität und Erneuerung über längere Zeit nebeneinander bestehen können – damit Neues wachsen kann, ohne das Bestehende zu entwerten. New Work ist dabei weder Selbstzweck noch Maßnahmenkatalog. Es kann dann einen Beitrag zu resilienter Transformation leisten, wenn es Rahmenbedingungen schafft, in denen Menschen Verantwortung übernehmen, gemeinsam lernen und Wandel gestalten. Hochschulen werden nicht zukunftsfähig, weil sie möglichst viele New-Work-Maßnahmen einführen. Sie werden zukunftsfähig, wenn sie lernen, Wandel gemeinsam zu gestalten.

Anne Prill ist seit 2017 Projektmanagerin für das Hochschulforum Digitalisierung beim CHE Centrum für Hochschulentwicklung. Als Transformationsdesignerin ist sie vor allem für die Themen „Zukunftsorientierte Lernräume“ und „New Work an Hochschulen“ zuständig. Dazu veröffentlicht sie HFD-Arbeitspapiere sowie Artikel und hält Keynotes auf verschiedenen Veranstaltungen. Außerdem initiierte sie das Tandem-Programm „HFDlead“, bei dem sie bundesweit Hochschulleitungen miteinander vernetzt und begleitet. Sie studierte Betriebswirtschaftslehre an der University of Sunderland und Wirtschaft, Europapolitik und Recht an der TH Wildau. Berufsbegleitend absolvierte sie zudem ihren Masterabschluss in Erwachsenenbildung an der TU Kaiserslautern. Seit September 2024 ist sie zertifizierte systemische Transformationsbegleiterin.

title: Gesundheitsvorsorge: „Viele ärztliche Leistungen werden indirekt rationiert“
summary: Schwangerenvorsorge, Osteoporose, Krebsfrüherkennung: Ärztliche Leistungen werden künftig anders vergütet. Ärzte und Ökonomen sorgen sich – für Frauen könnte das gravierende Folgen haben.

Von

26.11.2026, 08:21Lesezeit: 7 Min.

Zusammenfassung

Zum 1. Januar 2027 sollen bisher extrabudgetär vergütete ambulante Leistungen, darunter kurzfristige TSVG-Termine, in ein gedeckeltes Budget überführt werden, was nach Experten die Terminlage besonders in der Frauenmedizin verschärfen könnte.

Die Gesundheitsökonomin Professor Silke Arnegger von der Hochschule RheinMain sagt, Leistungen würden zwar nicht gestrichen, müssten aber künftig noch umfangreicher als bisher aus einem begrenzten Budget bezahlt werden.

title: Diploma Superior en Comunicación y Análisis Político
summary:
Convenio de CLACSO y Le Monde diplomatique, edición Cono Sur

La entrada Diploma Superior en Comunicación y Análisis Político se publicó primero en CLACSO.
full_text:
El miércoles 25 de noviembre el Consejo Latinoamericano de Ciencias Sociales y Le Monde diplomatique, edición Cono Sur, firmaron un convenio de colaboración para el diseño, organización e implementación de un Diploma Superior en Comunicación y Análisis Político, previsto para el año 2027.

Participaron por CLACSO su Director Ejecutivo Pablo Vommaro, su Directora de Producción Editorial Fernanda Pampín, y su Director de Formación y Red de Posgrados Alejandro Gambina; y por Le Monde diplomatique, edición Cono Sur, su director José Natanson, además del coordinador del Diploma Superior en Comunicación y Análisis Político Rodrigo Lloret.

La iniciativa se desarrolla en el marco de una alianza institucional entre ambas entidades, basada en la cooperación y el trabajo conjunto, y en el reconocimiento de sus respectivas trayectorias y capacidades académicas y de comunicación. La propuesta estará orientada a brindar herramientas de análisis, escritura y producción periodística para la elaboración de textos de opinión e intervención pública en los medios de comunicación y redes sociales.

El Diploma Superior se desarrollará en modalidad virtual, con una duración prevista de cuatro meses, entre abril y julio de 2027, y contempla doce encuentros, incluyendo actividades sincrónicas de apertura y cierre, ocho instancias de taller y discusión de producciones de las y los participantes, y dos clases a cargo de docentes invitados.

Al término de la firma, Pablo Vommaro manifestó estar “muy contento de esta alianza, de este acuerdo entre Le Monde diplomatique, edición Cono Sur, y CLACSO para impulsar juntos propuestas de formación de alta calidad, de incidencia pública, para poder trabajar desde las ciencias sociales, las humanidades y las artes, en este caso en la comunicación pública, en el análisis político y en el análisis periodístico, para que se puedan traducir las investigaciones, las producciones académicas en piezas de intervención pública, en piezas que produzcan incidencia en la conversación pública. Anunciamos esta nueva alianza como una forma de lograr incidencia política y pública y de articular rigurosidad en la producción académica con compromiso en los debates públicos”.

A su vez, José Natanson aportó que “estamos firmando el convenio de lanzamiento de la primera diplomatura entre CLACSO y Le Monde diplomatique. La idea es ofrecer a gente que quiere intervenir en los medios de comunicación, participar de la conversación pública y del análisis político, herramientas para poder aportar de alguna forma con columnas de opinión en los diarios, con artículos de análisis o escritura periodística.”

title: Giovani e AI, l’Italia indietro nella UE: cosa manca alla formazione
summary:
Il 72% degli studenti delle superiori usa l’IA per lo studio o nella vita personale. Una quota identica chiede di imparare a usarla. Dai limiti delle etichette previste dall’AI Act ai corsi delle Big Tech, il nodo è chi insegna a giudicarne le risposte

L'articolo Giovani e AI, l’Italia indietro nella UE: cosa manca alla formazione proviene da Agenda Digitale.
full_text:
L’Italia è fra gli ultimi Paesi europei per uso e comprensione dell’intelligenza artificiale generativa, e il ritardo riguarda soprattutto i più giovani. L’AI Act si propone di proteggere cittadini che spesso non possiedono le competenze basilari dello strumento, senza però prevedere chi debba formarli.

Ricostruiamo questa asimmetria, mettendo in luce come scuola e università non riescano a colmarla e come le piattaforme ne occupino lo spazio, e auspicando una politica strutturale di AI literacy negli anni formativi.

AI literacy in Italia: il divario con l’Europa

Nel novembre 2022, con il rilascio pubblico di ChatGPT, l’intelligenza artificiale generativa è uscita dai laboratori ed è entrata rapidamente nelle pratiche ordinarie della popolazione: dalla stesura di una mail di lavoro alla preparazione di un esame universitario, dalla ricerca di un’informazione alla sintesi di un articolo che non si ha il tempo – o la voglia – di leggere.

In poco più di due anni ce la si è ritrovata negli strumenti di uso comune: nei primi mesi del 2025 Microsoft l’ha inclusa negli abbonamenti domestici di Word, Excel e Outlook; Google ha affiancato ai risultati delle ricerche degli utenti italiani riepiloghi generati dall’intelligenza artificiale e Apple l’ha resa disponibile in italiano su tutti i suoi dispositivi (Apple, 2025; Budaraju, 2025; Rognier, 2025).

Nello stesso periodo Meta ha inserito il proprio assistente in WhatsApp, che in Italia conta circa trentasette milioni di utenti, e l’Autorità garante della concorrenza e del mercato, nell’avviare un’istruttoria nei confronti dell’azienda, ha osservato che il servizio è stato “reso autonomamente disponibile agli utenti senza che questi si siano attivati in tal senso” (Autorità Garante della Concorrenza e del Mercato [AGCM], 2025, par. 4). I chatbot sono così divenuti interlocutori quotidiani, ai quali si chiede di spiegare, riassumere, tradurre e consigliare, tanto consueti da passare oggi quasi inosservati a chi se ne serve.

Tuttavia, si è cominciato a usare questi strumenti prima di sapere che cosa realmente fossero, e l’uso quotidiano, che pure rende familiare il dialogo con un chatbot, non garantisce le conoscenze necessarie a servirsene correttamente, seppur possa dare l’illusione di possederle. Un chatbot restituisce, infatti, risposte fluide, ordinate e formulate con sicurezza (Grimaldi, 2026), sicché il buon esito di una richiesta finisce per essere scambiato per una prova della propria competenza, mentre a venir meno è proprio la capacità di monitorare e valutare i propri processi cognitivi, ciò che la psicologia chiama metacognizione (Flavell, 1979; Nelson & Narens, 1990).

Lo scarto è stato documentato anche sperimentalmente: chiamati a risolvere con ChatGPT una serie di problemi di ragionamento logico tratti dal test di ammissione alle law school statunitensi, i partecipanti hanno migliorato i propri risultati ma hanno sopravvalutato la propria prestazione, e la valutazione di sé è risultata meno accurata proprio fra chi si attribuiva maggiori conoscenze sull’intelligenza artificiale (Fernandes et al., 2026).

L’AI literacy (intesa come l’insieme delle competenze che consentono di valutare criticamente le tecnologie di intelligenza artificiale, di comunicare e collaborare efficacemente con esse e di servirsene come strumento in rete, a casa e sul lavoro, secondo la definizione di Long & Magerko, 2020), infatti, non si riduce alla capacità di usare questi strumenti, bensì è una competenza che va coltivata, fatta di comprensione del loro funzionamento e di giudizio critico, e che dalla semplice pratica non discende automaticamente (Laupichler et al., 2022).

La distanza fra familiarità e comprensione riguarda chiunque, ma pesa soprattutto su chi incontra l’intelligenza artificiale mentre si formano le proprie abitudini di studio, di lavoro e di informazione, e chiama in causa anzitutto la scuola, cioè l’istituzione cui spetterebbe trasformare quelle abitudini in competenza.

Proprio dagli studenti, del resto, arriva la richiesta più esplicita. Le risposte raccolte dal Censis fra chi frequenta la scuola secondaria di secondo grado restituiscono l’intelligenza artificiale come una presenza ormai ordinaria della giornata, dentro e fuori dalle aule, tanto che il 72,0% dichiara di servirsene per lo studio o nella vita personale.

Eppure una quota identica, convinta che “l’utilizzo esperto dell’Ia è una competenza fondamentale per il futuro” (Censis, 2025, par. 2), ritiene che quell’uso debba diventare oggetto di insegnamento, sicché a chiedere di imparare a usare l’intelligenza artificiale è una popolazione che in larga parte già se ne serve.

Quanto usano l’IA generativa i giovani italiani

Si tratta di una richiesta che proviene, d’altronde, da un Paese che nell’adozione di questi strumenti resta indietro rispetto al resto d’Europa: secondo Eurostat, nel 2025 il 42,6% degli italiani fra i sedici e i ventinove anni ha utilizzato almeno uno strumento di intelligenza artificiale generativa nei tre mesi precedenti la rilevazione, a fronte di una media europea del 60,4%, e fra i ventisette Stati membri soltanto la Romania si colloca più in basso, con il 38,3%.

Né il divario si limita ai più giovani, poiché sull’intera popolazione fra i sedici e i settantaquattro anni la quota italiana si ferma al 19,9%, quasi tredici punti percentuali sotto il 32,7% della media dell’Unione (Eurostat, 2026a).

Il ritardo, del resto, non riguarda soltanto l’impiego pratico dello strumento, bensì, come si è detto, la conoscenza che se ne ha, o almeno che si ritiene di averne. Da alcuni anni Ipsos chiede ai cittadini di trentadue Paesi quanto pensino di capire l’intelligenza artificiale: nella rilevazione condotta fra marzo e aprile 2026 il 54% degli italiani dichiara di averne una buona comprensione, contro una media del 72%, e fra i dieci Stati dell’Unione inclusi nel campione l’Italia occupa l’ultima posizione, sette punti sotto la Germania (Ipsos, 2026).

Resta da chiarire, allora, a chi spetti formare quella competenza: il regolamento europeo sull’intelligenza artificiale (Regolamento UE 2024/1689), il cosiddetto AI Act, ha scelto di proteggere i cittadini anzitutto informandoli, obbligando chi diffonde questi sistemi a dichiarare quando si dialoga con una macchina o si ha davanti un contenuto generato (art. 50), e dà così per scontato che chi riceve l’avvertimento sappia interpretarlo.

L’obbligo di alfabetizzazione vale invece soltanto per il personale che imprese ed enti incaricano di utilizzare questi sistemi (art. 4) e lascia fuori chi se ne serve da sé, come accade agli studenti e a molti giovani lavoratori, mentre in Italia le politiche rivolte a questa popolazione sono arrivate tardi e passano per lo più da iniziative facoltative delle scuole (D.Lgs. 179/2026, artt. 36-38).

Si delinea così un’asimmetria normativa: si è pensato, infatti, al mittente e alle sue responsabilità, imponendogli di rendere riconoscibile ciò che diffonde, mentre si è lasciato indietro il destinatario, cui si chiede di comprendere senza che nessuno gli abbia insegnato a farlo.

Il compito di formare quel destinatario ricade dunque, di fatto, sulla media literacy, cioè sulla capacità di accedere ai messaggi mediali, di analizzarli, valutarli e produrli (Livingstone, 2004), che deve oggi estendersi anche ai contenuti generati e ai sistemi che li producono. L’articolo ricostruisce questa asimmetria e discute se e a quali condizioni la media literacy possa farsene carico.

AI Act ed etichette: le competenze per valutare i contenuti

Il primo requisito per orientarsi in un mondo in cui contenuti generati circolano accanto a quelli prodotti da persone è saperli distinguere, cioè riconoscere che cosa è stato prodotto dall’intelligenza artificiale e che cosa no. È su questa capacità che l’AI Act fa affidamento quando sceglie di proteggere i cittadini attraverso l’etichettatura di questi contenuti.

L’idea che basti avvertire il pubblico per proteggerlo non nasce con l’AI Act, bensì con una tradizione che nel corso del Novecento ha fatto della trasparenza uno strumento di governo, dalle leggi sull’accesso agli atti pubblici alle informazioni obbligatorie sulle confezioni, fino alle etichette nutrizionali (Ananny & Crawford, 2018).

In ciascuno di questi casi chi produce un bene o esercita un potere è tenuto a renderlo visibile, mentre a chi riceve l’informazione spetta il compito di capirla e di trarne le conseguenze: è lo stesso schema dell’art. 50 dell’AI Act, in cui il mittente dichiara l’impiego di strumenti AI e il destinatario viene, così, informato.

Il limite di questo schema sta nel confondere l’essere informati con il comprendere ciò che sta dietro l’informazione, e nel lasciare al singolo l’onere di interpretarla, come se il pubblico fosse per definizione in grado di farlo (Ananny & Crawford, 2018). La trasparenza protegge dunque soltanto chi è in grado di leggerla, e presuppone un pubblico che nessuno, come si è visto, si incarica di formare.

Il divario nelle competenze informative

Le rilevazioni europee sulle competenze digitali permettono di guardare più da vicino il destinatario che l’AI Act presuppone, almeno nella sua parte più giovane: Eurostat misura queste competenze in cinque domini (informazione, comunicazione, creazione di contenuti, sicurezza, soluzione di problemi) e classifica il livello di ciascun intervistato in base al numero e al tipo di attività che dichiara di svolgere. Nel complesso i 16-29enni italiani non sono indietro rispetto ai coetanei europei, poiché chi possiede competenze superiori a quelle di base è il 43,2%, contro il 43,5% della media dell’Unione (Eurostat, 2026b).

Il quadro cambia se si guarda al dominio che più riguarda la lettura di un contenuto generato, quello che riguarda le competenze informative, ossia la capacità di cercare informazioni, valutarne l’attendibilità e gestirle. Qui le competenze superiori alla base raggiungono il 68,4% dei giovani italiani, contro il 79,8% dei coetanei europei, con uno scarto di oltre undici punti percentuali. Il ritardo, quindi, riguarda nello specifico la capacità di giudicare ciò che si trova in rete, e farlo, d’altronde, richiede due ordini di competenze, critiche e tecniche, che soltanto insieme permettono di valutare efficacemente un contenuto.
